donuts.name: Classic Glazed
donuts.history: The ring doughnut’s origin story usually points to Rockport, Maine, where Captain Hanson Gregory said he punched out the soggy middle in 1847. Dutch olykoeks (“oil cakes”) had already arrived with New Amsterdam settlers, but the hole made frying even and created the American ring. By the early 1900s, automated doughnut machines and thin sugar glaze turned the shiny yeast ring into a breakfast staple from New York counters to West Coast shops — glaze sealing moisture so the crumb stays soft for hours.
donuts.avatarScript: Classic Glazed is the handshake of the donut world — yeast dough, hot oil, and a glassy vanilla coat.

origin.note: Captain Hanson Gregory claimed inventing the ring doughnut by knocking out the soggy center.

donuts.name: Boston Cream
donuts.history: Boston cream pie (really a cake) became a Massachusetts pride dish in the 1800s: sponge, vanilla custard, chocolate top. Bakers later compressed that idea into a filled yeast doughnut — custard piped inside, chocolate ganache on top. By the mid-20th century it was a New England bakery fixture and a Dunkin’-era classic nationwide, a portable echo of Boston’s favorite “pie.”
donuts.avatarScript: Boston Cream is dessert cosplay: vanilla custard inside, chocolate on top.

origin.note: Named for Boston cream pie — custard + chocolate — remade as a filled yeast doughnut.

donuts.name: Raspberry Jelly
donuts.history: Jelly doughnuts descend from Central and Eastern European fried filled pastries — German Berliners, Polish pączki — brought into North American bakeries by immigrant bakers. Powdered sugar hides the surprise; raspberry’s bright acid cuts rich fried dough. In the U.S. they became carnival and bakery-case standards, especially around holidays and Sunday mornings.
donuts.avatarScript: Raspberry Jelly is the plot twist donut — quiet powdered exterior, then a berry burst.

origin.note: Cousin to Berliners and Polish pączki; jelly-filled rounds crossed the Atlantic with immigrant bakers.

donuts.name: Old-Fashioned
donuts.history: Unlike puffy yeast rings, old-fashioned cake donuts use chemical leavening and often sour cream for tenderness. The cracked, craggy surface isn’t a flaw — it’s the signature that holds thick glaze in little pools. Midwestern and neighborhood American bakeries perfected the style in the early 1900s as a denser, dunkable cousin to the yeast raised ring.
donuts.avatarScript: Old-Fashioned is the crunchy-edged cousin — cake crumb, nutmeg hush, glaze in every crack.

origin.note: Sour-cream cake rings with craggy cracks — denser than yeast, built to catch glaze pools.

donuts.name: Maple Walnut
donuts.history: Maple sugar and syrup are rooted in Indigenous foodways across the northeastern woodlands. Colonial and New England sugarhouses later commercialized the spring sap run. Bakeries turned that forest sweetness into maple glaze; toasted walnuts add crunch that echoes Vermont and Canadian sugar-shack seasons more than tropical fruit shops.
donuts.avatarScript: Maple Walnut tastes like autumn trees — sticky maple shine and walnut crunch.

origin.note: Maple syrup has deep Indigenous roots; New England bakeries turned it into cold-weather glaze.

donuts.name: French Cruller
donuts.history: “Cruller” names vary, but the French-style ring uses pâte à choux — the same cooked dough behind éclairs and cream puffs — piped with a star tip so ridges catch a light glaze. It fries hollow and airy, a European pastry technique that found a second life in North American doughnut cases as the lightest bite in the box.
donuts.avatarScript: French Cruller is the ballerina of the case — choux dough and a glaze that almost floats.

origin.note: Ridged rings of choux pastry — the same airy dough family as éclairs — fried and lightly glazed.

donuts.name: Chocolate Frosted
donuts.history: Once American doughnut shops scaled yeast rings, thick chocolate frosting beat thin glaze for holding sprinkles. Mid-century counters and national chains made the cocoa crown + candy jimmies a childhood default — less about Old World pastry lineage, more about soda-fountain color and Saturday mornings.
donuts.avatarScript: Chocolate Frosted is pure celebration energy — cocoa hat and a confetti of sprinkles.

origin.note: Thick cocoa frosting + sprinkles became the kid-counter classic once chains scaled yeast rings.

donuts.name: Strawberry Sprinkle
donuts.history: Pink strawberry frosting is a mid-century American bakery color language — soda fountains, birthday boxes, and “fun” frosting long before Instagram. The flavor is often strawberry puree or oil in a sweet frosting base; sprinkles turn it into weekend energy on a classic yeast ring.
donuts.avatarScript: Strawberry Sprinkle is Glazed’s pink wink — berry frost and a sparkle of candy.

origin.note: Bright pink frost rode mid-century soda-fountain color — bakery shorthand for “fun” long before social media.

donuts.name: Lemon Poppy
donuts.history: Lemon and poppy seed traveled with Central European baking (think Austrian and Hungarian cakes) into American morning pastry. Citrus oil brightens fried dough; tiny poppy seeds add nutty crunch. It reads sunny and bakery-European even when sold beside chocolate-frosted American classics.
donuts.avatarScript: Lemon Poppy wakes up the case — sunshine glaze and tiny seed crackle.

origin.note: Lemon and poppy seed traveled with Central European baking into sunny American morning cases.

donuts.name: Apple Fritter
donuts.history: Fritters are older than tidy rings — irregular fried dough studded with fruit. American fairgrounds and orchard belts (Pennsylvania, Ohio, New England) made apple fritters a cold-weather and carnival favorite: cinnamon, chunks of apple, and a glaze that clings to every jagged edge.
donuts.avatarScript: Apple Fritter breaks the ring rule — crispy edges, soft apple pockets, sticky glaze.

origin.note: Irregular fried apple dough — carnival and orchard country energy more than tidy ring geometry.

donuts.name: Cinnamon Sugar
donuts.history: Cinnamon-sugar coatings echo Spanish and colonial New World sweets (think churros and spiced fried dough). U.S. shops made the warm sugar shake a simple classic — no frosting required — just spice, crunch, and heat from the fryer.
donuts.avatarScript: Cinnamon Sugar is cozy minimalism — warm spice that sticks to your fingers.

origin.note: Cinnamon-sugar coatings echo Spanish and colonial sweets; American shops made the warm shake iconic.

donuts.name: Matcha White Chocolate
donuts.history: Matcha’s home is Japanese tea culture; late 20th- and 21st-century cafés folded it into global pastry. On a doughnut, grassy umami meets sweet white chocolate so the tea note stays friendly. It’s a modern fusion case item — Kyoto green meeting American fryer tradition.
donuts.avatarScript: Matcha White Chocolate is the modern looker — jade glaze with a sweet white drizzle.

origin.note: Matcha moved from tea ceremony into modern pastry; white chocolate softens the grassy bitterness.

donuts.name: Blueberry Cake
donuts.history: Wild lowbush blueberries shaped Maine and Northeast baking — muffins, pies, and cake crumbs. Blueberry cake doughnuts borrow that orchard-and-coast pantry: tender cake crumb, berry pockets, and a nod to summer markets along the Downeast shore.
donuts.avatarScript: Blueberry Cake is the baker’s dozen lucky extra — purple-kissed cake crumb.

origin.note: Wild blueberries shaped Northeastern cake tradition — crumb cake energy in doughnut form.

smoothies.name: Mango Sunrise

ingredients: ¾ cup orange juice or coconut milk
steps: Add liquid to reach a thick sip.
Pour cold and serve with a straw.

smoothies.history: Mango smoothies rode the 1990s–2000s juice-bar boom — ripe mango’s natural sweetness needs little sugar, so the drink stays bright and thick.
smoothies.avatarScript: Mango Sunrise is liquid sunshine — thick gold you can drink beside a warm donut.

smoothies.name: Berry Blast

ingredients: ¾ cup apple juice or milk
steps: Blend until smooth and vivid purple-red.
Taste for tartness; sweeten lightly if needed.

smoothies.history: Berry blends became smoothie-bar staples for color and punchy flavor — a tart counterpoint to sweet bakery cases.
smoothies.avatarScript: Berry Blast is the bold cup — deep berry color that wakes up the counter.

smoothies.name: Tropical Green

steps: Add fruit and blend until bright green.

smoothies.history: Green smoothies popularized veggies-in-a-cup in the 2010s — pineapple and banana keep spinach friendly for first-timers.
smoothies.avatarScript: Tropical Green is the sneaky healthy one — paradise flavor with a leafy wink.

smoothies.name: Strawberry Banana

steps: Pour and garnish with a berry if you like.

smoothies.history: Strawberry-banana is the gateway smoothie — soft fruit, familiar sweetness, and the drink most people order first at a donut-and-smoothie counter.
smoothies.avatarScript: Strawberry Banana is the classic handshake of the smoothie board — pink, creamy, forever.

smoothies.name: Cookies & Cream

ingredients: 2 cups vanilla ice cream or frozen yogurt
steps: Blend milk, ice cream, and vanilla until smooth.
Pulse in cookies so you still get crunchy bits.
Pour and top with cookie crumbs.

smoothies.history: Cookies-and-cream jumped from ice cream aisles into blender bars — a dessert cup that fits right beside a glazed donut case.
smoothies.avatarScript: Cookies & Cream is the dessert twin of the board — creamy, cookie-crunch, zero regrets.

smoothies.name: PB Banana Cocoa
smoothies.tagline: Peanut butter hug in a cup

steps: Taste for sweetness; add honey if needed.
Serve with a peanut-butter swirl if you’re feeling fancy.

smoothies.history: Peanut butter–banana drinks grew up in home kitchens and gyms, then landed on smoothie boards as the filling, savory-sweet option next to fruit cups.
smoothies.avatarScript: PB Banana Cocoa is the power hug — nutty, chocolatey, and perfect after a maple donut.
